about: Oldest songs and written music, instruments, hymns, carols and anthems, recordings and performances of the British Isles, each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Sumer is icumen in
entries.claim: the oldest known musical composition in six-part polyphony: a round in Middle English
entries.evidence: The round survives in British Library Harley MS 978, a miscellany from Reading Abbey (or its cell at Leominster) copied in the early 1260s. It is the oldest known piece written for six parts (four voices in canon over a two-part pes). Its composer is unknown; W. de Wycombe and John of Fornsete are suggestions, not established.

entries.name: Winchester Troper
entries.age_text: 11th century; the core of Corpus 473 probably copied in the 1020s-1030s
entries.claim: the largest surviving collection of 11th-century polyphony, among the oldest written part-music in Europe
entries.evidence: Two Winchester manuscripts make up the Troper; only Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 473 has polyphony, 174 two-voice organa written apart from their chants. Its dating has moved from about 1000 to the 1020s-1030s. The neumes give no exact pitches, so modern performances are reconstructions.

entries.name: Robert ap Huw manuscript
entries.age_text: copied c. 1613; the pieces date from between 1340 and 1500
entries.claim: the oldest written Welsh music, and claimed to be the oldest notated harp music in Europe
entries.evidence: Robert ap Huw of Anglesey copied the music around 1613 in a tablature of his own tradition, from the lost manuscript of the harper William Penllyn. The pieces of cerdd dant it holds are dated between about 1340 and 1500; the title's claim that its rules were settled under Gruffudd ap Cynan about 1100 is not accepted as fact. The 'oldest notated harp music in Europe' claim comes from a Welsh music centre, not a survey.

entries.name: Wicklow Pipes
entries.claim: the oldest known wooden pipes in the world, found in Ireland
entries.evidence: Six yew tubes were found in 2003 in a wood-lined trough during a rescue excavation at Charlesland, Co. Wicklow, and dated by radiocarbon to the end of the Stone Age or start of the Bronze Age. They are taken to be a set of pipes, but whether they were played as musical instruments is an interpretation of the find. Bone flutes found elsewhere in Europe are far older; the claim is for wooden pipes.

entries.name: Queen Mary Harp
entries.age_text: frame radiocarbon dated to the 14th or early 15th century (cal AD 1302-1413)
entries.claim: the oldest dated surviving European harp
entries.evidence: This Gaelic clarsach from the West Highlands was long dated to the 15th century by its carving; radiocarbon dating of all three frame timbers, funded by the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, put them in the 14th or early 15th century. No other early clarsach has been dated by analysis, so the Lamont Harp (also in Edinburgh) and the Trinity College harp in Dublin may be as old. The story that Mary, Queen of Scots gave it away in 1563 is family tradition.

entries.name: Trinity College harp (Brian Boru harp)
entries.claim: the oldest surviving Irish harp; it did not belong to Brian Boru
entries.evidence: The harp is one of the three surviving medieval Gaelic harps, with the Queen Mary and Lamont harps in Edinburgh. Its link to Brian Boru (d. 1014), published in the 18th century, was dismissed by George Petrie in 1840 as a forgery, and Trinity's library calls the association mistaken. It has not been dated by radiocarbon; dates on style range from the 14th to the 15th century.

entries.name: Hymn to St Magnus (Nobilis, humilis)
entries.claim: the oldest surviving Scottish choral music, a two-part hymn from Orkney
entries.evidence: The hymn honours St Magnus, Earl of Orkney (killed about 1117), and survives only in a manuscript at Uppsala University in Sweden. It is sung in two parts moving mostly in parallel thirds. Its date is given as the 12th or the 13th century, and its 'oldest Scottish' standing rests on reviews and summaries rather than a published survey.

entries.name: Wexford Carol
entries.age_text: 15th or 16th century on its style; sometimes said to be 12th century
entries.claim: said to be Ireland's oldest known Christmas carol; its age is unsettled
entries.evidence: The carol from Enniscorthy became known after the organist William Grattan Flood took it down from a local singer and had it printed in The Oxford Book of Carols (1928). A 12th-century origin is repeated widely, but its music and words point to the 15th or 16th century, and some editors think the text is English in origin. No early manuscript is known.

entries.name: God Save the King
entries.age_text: tune first printed 1744; words printed and first sung in public in 1745
entries.claim: the British national anthem, first printed in 1744 (the tune) and 1745 (the words)
entries.evidence: The often-quoted date of 1745 is when the song was sung at the London theatres during the Jacobite rising and printed in The Gentleman's Magazine; a version for two voices had already appeared in Thesaurus Musicus in 1744. Words and tune are anonymous, and claims for older authors (John Bull, Henry Carey and others) are unproven.

entries.name: Handel Festival recording of Israel in Egypt
entries.claim: the earliest surviving deliberate recording of music, and the oldest surviving recording made in Britain
entries.evidence: Colonel George Gouraud, Edison's agent in London, recorded a chorus of some 4,000 voices at the Crystal Palace Handel Festival on wax cylinders from about 100 yards away; the cylinders are in the Thomas Edison National Historical Park. Until 2009 it was thought the oldest recorded voice; the 1860 phonautograph of 'Au clair de la lune' is older but was not made to be played back. Recordings made in the 1870s on tinfoil are lost.

entries.name: Sullivan's The Lost Chord on the phonograph
entries.age_text: c. August 1888 (played to the press on 14 August 1888)
entries.claim: one of the first recordings of music ever made, and among the oldest recordings made in Britain
entries.evidence: Gouraud played a cornet and piano recording of Arthur Sullivan's song 'The Lost Chord' when he introduced Edison's improved phonograph to the London press on 14 August 1888; the cylinder is kept by the Edison National Historical Park. On 5 October 1888 Sullivan himself recorded a message to Edison at Gouraud's house, 'Little Menlo', which also survives. The Handel Festival cylinders of June 1888 are older.

entries.name: York Mystery Plays
entries.claim: one of the four nearly complete English mystery play cycles, recorded in York from 1376 and played again today
entries.evidence: The 48 pageants were staged by the York craft guilds on wagons at Corpus Christi from the 14th century until they were suppressed in 1569; the first record is from 1376, when the wagons were already in use. Their manuscript of about 1463-1477 survives in the British Library. Chester, Towneley (Wakefield) and N-Town cycles are of similar age, and Coventry's pageants are recorded from 1392.

entries.name: The Pride of Life
entries.age_text: written on an account roll of 1343-1344; usually dated to the later 14th century
entries.claim: the earliest known morality play in English, written down in Dublin
entries.evidence: The play was copied on the back of an account roll of the Priory of the Holy Trinity (Christ Church), Dublin, for 1343-1344; the roll was destroyed in the Public Record Office fire of 1922, so it is known from an 1891 transcription. The text breaks off mid-line. The play itself may be later than the roll; Hildegard of Bingen's Latin Ordo Virtutum is a far older morality play.
